name: Eguchi-Hanson Space
description: A space of four dimensions with no time in it, the gravitational instanton Tohru Eguchi and Andrew Hanson found in 1978: a solution of Einstein's vacuum equations with Riemannian signature and self dual curvature. Space closes on a 2-sphere of radius $a/2$, the bolt, and far away it is flat space with every point identified with its opposite.
convention: The length $a$ is the space's only parameter. All four coordinates are spatial, so no component carries a factor of $c$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What does an instanton of gravity look like? Alexander Belavin, Alexander Polyakov, Albert Schwarz, and Yu.S. Tyupkin had found the first instantons in 1975, in Yang-Mills theory: "regular solutions of the four dimensional euclidean Yang-Mills equations", with finite action [bpst1975]. Stephen Hawking carried the idea over to gravity two years later and named two candidates, the Schwarzschild and Taub-NUT solutions with time turned into a fourth direction of space, "the latter being self-dual" [hawking1977]. Tohru Eguchi, at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, and Andrew Hanson, at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory, were postdocs who met in the fall of 1977 and wanted a closer copy [eguchihanson1978, hanson2020]. A Yang-Mills instanton "approaches a pure gauge at infinity", so gravity's ought to flatten out in all four directions, and Hawking's Taub-NUT metrics "do not approach a flat metric at infinity" [eguchihanson1978].¶Their recipe was the Yang-Mills one: ask for a self dual curvature, build the metric from the 3-spheres around a centre with a function of the radius left free, and solve what is left [eguchihanson1979]. Self duality leaves a first order equation for one function of the radius, and its solution carries one constant of integration, the length $a$ [eguchihanson1978]. In Euler angles on the 3-sphere the metric is $$ds^2 = \left(1 - \frac{a^4}{r^4}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + \frac{r^2}{4}\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right) + \frac{r^2}{4}\left(1 - \frac{a^4}{r^4}\right)\left(d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\phi\right)^2,$$ which at $a = 0$ is flat space in polar coordinates [gibbonshawking1979, eguchihanson1979]. All four coordinates are spatial: the metric is Riemannian, of signature $(+,+,+,+)$, a solution of Einstein's vacuum equations with no time in it and no light cones [eguchihanson1978]. Its curvature dies away as $1/r^6$, where that of Taub-NUT and Schwarzschild falls like $1/r^3$, which suggested to Eguchi and Hanson "that our metrics describe gravitational 'dipoles'" [eguchihanson1978]. They read it as a sign that their solutions "will not have a meaningful continuation to Minkowski space" [eguchihanson1978].¶The trouble sat at $r = a$, where the first term blows up [eguchihanson1978]. By Hanson's account of 2020, early in 1978 they "did not publish because there was something wrong, a puzzling singularity", until Isadore Singer, shown the metric on a blackboard in Berkeley, "recognized our singularity as a standard problem with a standard solution in under a minute" [hanson2020]. The standard problem is the origin of polar coordinates: with $u^2 = r^2(1 - a^4/r^4)$ the metric near $r = a$ at fixed $\theta$ and $\phi$ is $\tfrac{1}{4}(du^2 + u^2d\psi^2)$, a flat plane, provided $\psi$ goes around once in $2\pi$ [eguchihanson1978, eguchihanson1979]. An Euler angle on a 3-sphere takes $4\pi$ to go around, and with that range the plane is a cone with its tip at $r = a$ [eguchihanson1979]. Halving the range identifies opposite points of every 3-sphere, so the boundary at infinity is "a three-sphere with opposite points identified", a result Eguchi and Hanson, writing with Peter Gilkey in 1980, credited to Vladimir Belinskii, Gary Gibbons, Don Page, and Christopher Pope [gibbonshawking1979, eguchigilkeyhanson1980, belinskii1978bianchi]. Eguchi and Hanson called such metrics "asymptotically locally Euclidean" [eguchihanson1979].¶And $r = a$ itself? It is a round 2-sphere of area $\pi a^2$, and the space has no points inside it [gibbonshawking1979, eguchihanson1979]. Gibbons and Hawking sorted the fixed points of a symmetry of such a space into "isolated points which we call 'nuts' and 2-surfaces which we call 'bolts'", the nut after Taub-NUT and the bolt "for obvious reasons", and the sphere $r = a$ is a bolt of the rotation in $\psi$ [gibbonshawking1979]. Over each point of the bolt stands a plane, covered by $r$ and $\psi$, which makes the whole space the cotangent bundle of the 2-sphere [eguchigilkeyhanson1980, eguchihanson1979]. "Nuts carry one unit of Euler characteristic, while bolts carry two units", so the Euler characteristic of the Eguchi-Hanson space is $2$, and its action is zero [eguchihanson1979].¶Eugenio Calabi reached the same metric from pure geometry, "as the solution to an abstract mathematical problem" [eguchigilkeyhanson1980]. In a lecture at the École Polytechnique on 5 June 1978 he built complete Kähler metrics with vanishing Ricci curvature on line bundles over spaces such as the complex projective spaces, and the simplest of them, over the projective line, is Eguchi and Hanson's in other coordinates [calabi1979]. Calabi said so himself, citing their letter [calabi1979]. Gibbons and Hawking came at it a third way the same year: drop the constant $1$ from the potential of Hawking's Taub-NUT solution with many centres, keep two centres, and "one obtains the Eguchi-Hanson metric" [gibbonshawking1978, gibbonshawking1979]. Eguchi and Hanson wrote that "it seems certain" the two metrics agree, and M. K. Prasad supplied the change of coordinates in 1979 [eguchihanson1979, prasad1979]. In Gibbons and Hawking's coordinates the two centres are the north and south poles of the bolt [ishihara2006].¶How far does the family go? As far as the finite subgroups of $SU(2)$: Nigel Hitchin conjectured that every asymptotically locally Euclidean space with self dual curvature belongs to one of them, and in 1989 Peter Kronheimer proved it [hitchin1979, hansonsha2017, kronheimer1989a, kronheimer1989b]. Eguchi and Hanson's space belongs to the smallest of them, whose one map sends every point to its opposite: it is flat space of two complex dimensions with opposite points identified and the origin replaced by the bolt [lebrun1988, kronheimer1989b]. Page used sixteen of them as plugs: a flat torus of four dimensions with opposite points identified has sixteen singular points, and with an Eguchi-Hanson space glued in at each it approximates the self dual metric on the K3 surface [page1978k3, gibbonspope1979]. Give the space a time and it can hold black holes, as the pair of charged ones that Hideki Ishihara, Masashi Kimura, Ken Matsuno, and Shinya Tomizawa set on it, one at each pole of the bolt [ishihara2006]. Hanson and Ji-Ping Sha found a surface of four dimensions in flat space of eleven with exactly this metric, and drew pictures of the space from it [hansonsha2017].

related.text: Continue Taub-NUT to Euclidean signature, give it the mass $M = L(1 + a^4/8L^4)$, and send its NUT parameter $L \to \infty$ with $r^2 = \rho^2 - L^2$ held fixed: the limit is the Eguchi-Hanson space, and the two share the isometry group $U(2)$ [eguchihanson1979, gibbonshawking1979].

The monopole's four dimensions of space are Gibbons and Hawking's metric with one centre and the constant $1$ kept in its potential. Drop the constant and take two centres, and the space is Eguchi and Hanson's [gibbonshawking1979, sorkin1983].

Majumdar and Papapetrou's black holes are built on a sum of potentials $1/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ over flat space, one for each hole. The Eguchi-Hanson space is built on the same sum with two terms, and its two centres are regular points [gibbonshawking1978, ishihara2006].

Schwarzschild's black hole continued to Euclidean signature is Hawking's first gravitational instanton, and its horizon is a bolt as well, Gibbons and Hawking's "canonical example" [hawking1977, gibbonshawking1979].

A universe whose three axes on the 3-sphere all differ, as the axes of Belinskii, Gibbons, Page, and Pope's self dual metrics do. Of those, the only one with no singularity has two axes equal and is the Eguchi-Hanson space [belinskii1978bianchi, eguchihanson1979].

Gibbons and Hawking's metrics of many centres, which stand among the gravitational instantons of 1977 and 1978. The Eguchi-Hanson space is their case of two centres with no constant in the potential [gibbonshawking1979, eguchigilkeyhanson1980].

coordinates.name: Eguchi-Hanson
domains: r = a \;\text{(the bolt, a 2-sphere of radius}\; a/2\text{)}

parameters.description: The space's one length: the bolt $r = a$ is a 2-sphere of radius $a/2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(r, \theta, \phi, \psi)$, with $r$ a length and $\theta$, $\phi$, and $\psi$ the Euler angles of the 3-sphere, $\psi$ with period $2\pi$. With the orientation $dr \wedge d\theta \wedge d\phi \wedge d\psi$ the Riemann tensor is self dual.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{2a^4}{r\left(r^4 - a^4\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r^4 - a^4}{4r^3}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^4 - a^4\right)\left(r^4 + a^4\cos^2\theta\right)}{4r^7}\dot{\phi}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^4 + a^4\right)\left(r^4 - a^4\right)\cos\theta}{2r^7}\dot{\phi}\dot{\psi} - \dfrac{\left(r^4 + a^4\right)\left(r^4 - a^4\right)}{4r^7}\dot{\psi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Kähler Radius

parameters.description: The space's one length: the bolt $\rho = 0$ is a 2-sphere of radius $a/2$
The square of Eguchi and Hanson's radius, $W = r^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi, \psi)$, with $\rho$ the radius of the flat space the metric approaches far from the bolt, $\rho^4 = r^4 - a^4$ in Eguchi and Hanson's radius $r$, and $\theta$, $\phi$, and $\psi$ the Euler angles of the 3-sphere.

coordinates.name: Gibbons-Hawking Two-Centre
domains: (\rho, z) = (0, \pm a) \;\text{(the two centres, regular points)}

parameters.description: The space's one length: the two centres stand at $z = \pm a$
The distance from the centre at $z = a$
The distance from the centre at $z = -a$

The potential whose curl is the gradient of $V$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\rho, z, \psi, \tau)$, with $\rho$, $z$, and $\psi$ cylindrical coordinates on a flat space of three dimensions and $\tau$ a length of period $\pi a/2$ around the circle over each of its points. In Eguchi and Hanson's coordinates $z = r^2\cos\theta/a$, $\rho = \sqrt{r^4 - a^4}\,\sin\theta/a$, and $\tau = a\phi/4$.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} - \dfrac{\rho\left(R_1^2 - R_1\,R_2 + R_2^2\right)}{2R_1^2\,R_2^2}\dot{\rho}^2 + \dfrac{\left(R_1 - R_2\right)\left(R_1^4 + R_1^3\,R_2 - 4a^2\,R_1^2 + R_1\,R_2^3 - 4a^2\,R_1\,R_2 + R_2^4 - 4a^2\,R_2^2\right)}{4a\,R_1^2\,R_2^2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)}\dot{\rho}\dot{z} + \dfrac{\rho\left(R_1^2 - R_1\,R_2 + R_2^2\right)}{2R_1^2\,R_2^2}\dot{z}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(R_1^2 + 2R_1\,R_2 + R_2^2 + 4a^2\right)}{2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^2}\dot{\psi}^2 + \dfrac{16\rho\left(R_1 - R_2\right)}{\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^2}\dot{\psi}\dot{\tau} - \dfrac{32\rho\left(R_1^2 - R_1\,R_2 + R_2^2\right)}{a^2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^2}\dot{\tau}^2 = 0

\ddot{z} - \dfrac{\left(R_1 - R_2\right)\left(R_1^4 + R_1^3\,R_2 - 4a^2\,R_1^2 + R_1\,R_2^3 - 4a^2\,R_1\,R_2 + R_2^4 - 4a^2\,R_2^2\right)}{8a\,R_1^2\,R_2^2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)}\dot{\rho}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(R_1^2 - R_1\,R_2 + R_2^2\right)}{R_1^2\,R_2^2}\dot{\rho}\dot{z} + \dfrac{\left(R_1 - R_2\right)\left(R_1^4 + R_1^3\,R_2 - 4a^2\,R_1^2 + R_1\,R_2^3 - 4a^2\,R_1\,R_2 + R_2^4 - 4a^2\,R_2^2\right)}{8a\,R_1^2\,R_2^2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)}\dot{z}^2 + \dfrac{\left(R_1 - R_2\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 + 2a\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 - 2a\right)\left(R_1^2 + 2R_1\,R_2 + R_2^2 + 4a^2\right)}{8a\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^3}\dot{\psi}^2 - \dfrac{4\left(R_1^2 + R_2^2\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 + 2a\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 - 2a\right)}{a\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^3}\dot{\psi}\dot{\tau} + \dfrac{8\left(R_1 - R_2\right)\left(R_1^4 + R_1^3\,R_2 - 4a^2\,R_1^2 + R_1\,R_2^3 - 4a^2\,R_1\,R_2 + R_2^4 - 4a^2\,R_2^2\right)}{a^3\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^3}\dot{\tau}^2 = 0

\ddot{\tau} + \dfrac{\left(R_1 - R_2\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 + 2a\right)^2\left(R_1 + R_2 - 2a\right)^2}{32\rho\,R_1\,R_2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^2}\dot{\rho}\dot{\psi} + \dfrac{\left(R_1^2 + R_2^2\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 + 2a\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 - 2a\right)}{2\rho\,R_1\,R_2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)^2}\dot{\rho}\dot{\tau} + \dfrac{a\left(R_1 + R_2 + 2a\right)\left(R_1 + R_2 - 2a\right)}{8R_1\,R_2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)}\dot{z}\dot{\psi} + \dfrac{2a\left(R_1 - R_2\right)}{R_1\,R_2\left(R_1 + R_2\right)}\dot{z}\dot{\tau} = 0
